newsitem.title: BURMA: Sanctions mar Burmese charm offensive.
newsitem.headline: Sanctions mar Burmese charm offensive.

text.p: A U.S. decision to slap sanctions on Burma has marred a public relations offensive launched by Rangoon but military leaders and diplomats on Wednesday shrugged off the immediate impact of the move.

News of the sanctions broke on Tuesday as dozens of foreign diplomats and journalists accompanied the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council's (SLORC) Secretary One, Khin Nyunt, on a tour of eastern Shan State, 550 km (330 miles) northeast of Rangoon.

The trip, through the notorious opium-growing Golden Triangle area, had been planned as a rare charm offensive to combat Western allegations of official complicity or inaction in regards to Burma's massive illegal narcotics trade.

Washington's sanctions stop U.S. firms from conducting new business in Burma as punishment for its failure "to cooperate in the war against drugs" as well as for its poor record on human rights, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in announcing the move.
"We don't feel very sorry about these sanctions because we have many friends in the region who understand us," Khin Nyunt told foreign journalists at an evening reception on Tuesday.
"In politics you have to expect such things. We have decided we will not stray (from our political cause)."
Smiling local villagers and former insurgents lined the streets of dusty towns as army helicopters swept into towns to disgorge their official entourage onto flag-bedecked streets.
The United States is the fourth-largest source of overseas investment in Burma. But diplomats and analysts said the immediate impact of the decision would be limited.
"The SLORC's not going to change easily," said a foreign official who declined to be identified. "Most of the U.S. firms have already pulled out, I don't think this will have much effect."
SLORC officials said the United States decision was not unexpected.
"We hoped for the best but we prepared for the worse," said Lieutenant Colonel Hla Min, adding that the decision to take action had been motivated by domestic U.S. politics.

Political instability and repression in Burma are seen as having worsened over the past year following a crackdown on student demonstrations, moves to further limit the moves of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi and recent reports of Buddhist-Moslem religious strife.

"It's definitely got worse," said a senior Western diplomat. "On their own, the NLD (Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy), the students or the monks probably couldn't do much but if any of these join forces then it could all blow up."
